samples.source: Today we'll consider why some wetlands contain remarkable archaeological remains, and why discovering those remains creates a new set of problems. When people imagine an ancient object surviving for centuries, they often think of stone or metal. In waterlogged settings, materials such as wood can sometimes remain where they would ordinarily decay. The important condition is not simply that the object is wet. Water can restrict the supply of oxygen, slowing some of the processes that normally destroy organic material. Conditions vary, so the presence of a wetland is not a guarantee that everything deposited there will survive.

samples.source: Think about buying a length of cloth from someone you have never met. The transaction requires more than agreement about price. You need a shared understanding of length. Today I'll discuss standard measures as a social arrangement as well as a technical achievement. A measure is useful when different people can reproduce it closely enough for the task. That does not mean every task needs the same precision. Selling cloth and testing an optical instrument place different demands on the system, even though both involve statements about distance.

samples.source: A discarded garment may look like a straightforward source of material, but recovering useful fibre requires a sequence of decisions. Today we'll follow a simplified mechanical recycling process for a stream of donated textiles. This is not a description of every industrial method. Different fabrics and desired outputs require different treatments. The point is to understand why collecting a large mass of clothing does not automatically create an equal mass of high-quality new cloth. Each stage changes what is available to the next, and some losses are unavoidable.

samples.source: A town trying to reduce household waste needs to know more than the weight arriving at a disposal site. It needs an account of what is discarded, where it comes from and which changes could realistically prevent it. Today we'll follow the design of a fictional waste audit. The first step is to define the boundary. Does the study cover homes only, or also restaurants and offices? If these sources are mixed without a record, a large quantity of food waste might be wrongly attributed to households when businesses produced much of it.

samples.source: A place name can remain familiar long after the feature it once described has disappeared. A street called Mill Lane may contain no mill, and a district named after a field may now be covered with houses. Today we'll consider how names can contribute to historical enquiry and why they should not be treated as complete records by themselves. Our examples come from an invented district, so the purpose is to explain a method rather than make claims about a particular real community's language or origins.

samples.source: A museum store is often imagined as a room full of objects waiting to appear in an exhibition. In practice, it is an information system with physical responsibilities. An object that is preserved perfectly but cannot be found is unavailable for research. An object that can be found but has lost its identity may be equally difficult to interpret. Today we'll follow the basic journey of an item entering a fictional local museum, concentrating on the connection between its physical location and its documentary record.
